Gameboard — eight desktop structures

Eight materially different ways to arrange the desktop board, all inside the shipped Petranaki world — same tokens, same chamfer, same rationed gold, same steel. Nothing here proposes a new look; the look is settled. What is being chosen is the arrangement.

Every board renders the same game state: Vader / Amnesty Housing against Luke / Data Vault, the board from the reference screenshot, down to Grogu’s five damage and the seventh Battle Droid. Card sizes, wrapping and crowding are therefore directly comparable between the eight.

Three card-level decisions are shared by concepts 2–8 so the layouts stay the only variable: damage is a wound meter rather than a disc stamped over the art; each upgrade is a named row with the stat delta it grants; and ownership is cool versus warm rather than green versus red, which stops the board fighting the Command and Aggression aspects. Concept 1 keeps the shipped treatment as the control.

1

Mirror Mat

Today’s arrangement, rebuilt properly rather than replaced. Space left, a leader/base spine down the centre, ground right, mirrored across a midline, stream on the right. It refuses nothing and risks nothing, which is exactly its job here: it is the control in the experiment.

One thing is deliberately left alone. C1 keeps the shipped centred damage disc so you can judge it directly against the wound meter every other card uses — look at Grogu in C1, then Grogu anywhere else.

  • Familiar
  • Lowest migration cost
  • Centre still holds the least-changing cards
  • Wide arenas still crush at the edges

2

Two Theatres

Stop splitting the screen by player and split it by arena. A full-width space theatre over a full-width ground theatre, each with its own midline and its own engagement. Leaders and bases move off the centre onto an outboard command pylon.

This is the only layout here that matches the rules topology: a unit only ever fights inside its own arena, so every attack becomes a short vertical hop instead of a diagonal across a spine. Your seven Battle Droids get 1 080px instead of 380px.

  • Rules-true topology
  • Solves arena crush outright
  • Full-width combat reading
  • Breaks 4 years of muscle memory
  • Leaders lose the centre

The Spine

A full-height glass command column down the centre owns both leaders, both bases, initiative, round, phase and the action buttons — everything that answers who, and whose turn. The two arenas become continuous vertical lanes either side, each holding both players.

The centre becomes the most-looked-at thing on the board instead of the least. You read by column: the whole space war on the left, the whole ground war on the right.

  • Turn state is finally findable
  • Arena identity is spatial
  • Narrow lanes at 7+ units
  • Centre column is heavy chrome

The Console

Asymmetric. You are not a second player on a shared table; you are the operator. A left command column owns everything of yours that is static — seat, resources, piles, leader, base, initiative, turn, stream — and the board itself carries no chrome at all.

The opponent gets one compact strip, because on your turn almost nothing about them changes. The 300px sidebar that today shows an empty log and a dash finally earns its width.

  • Sidebar earns its width
  • Board area is pure board
  • Opponent state is compressed
  • Asymmetry is disorienting in mirror matches

The Instrument Wall

Absolute positional constancy. Every zone is a labelled plate at a fixed grid box that never moves and never resizes, whatever the board holds. Overflow scrolls inside its plate instead of shoving a neighbour — so a seventh Battle Droid can never push your hand off-screen.

Between the two halves runs the engagement bar: round, phase, priority, initiative and the two actions, at the one place your eye already crosses. Corner brackets light on the plate that is live.

Built for the player who has played 500 games and wants their eye to land without searching.

  • Nothing ever moves
  • Overflow is contained, not destructive
  • Live-zone marker
  • Most chrome of the eight
  • Smallest cards

Focus Mat

The board spends its space on the decision in front of you. The arena you can act in runs at full size; the other collapses to a summary strip that still names every unit, its wound and its stats. One click re-opens it.

Shown here mid-game with ground live: the seven droids and Grogu are at 126px, while the space war — six units nobody is about to attack with — sits readable in 56px. Nothing is hidden; everything is proportioned.

  • Space goes where the decision is
  • Largest cards where it matters
  • Layout moves under you
  • Needs a rule for when to auto-switch

Clean Mat

The cards are the interface. No plates, no rails, no panels. An arena is a hairline and a tracked word set in the gutter; every piece of state collapses into two near-transparent edge bars.

Buys roughly 22% more card per pixel than any other layout here, and lets the card art and the aspect colours do the work the chrome is currently doing badly.

  • Biggest cards
  • Art and aspects read clearly
  • State is one glance further away
  • Log/chat has to become a drawer

8

Depth Table

Model the table. Your half sits forward, full size, under the key light; the opponent’s half recedes — smaller, cooler, dimmer, tipped away in Z — exactly as it does across a real table, with a lit table edge between you.

Depth carries ownership, so the green/red glows can go entirely: C8 is the only card here with no ownership tint at all, and the aspect colours on the cards get their contrast back.

  • Ownership without colour
  • Frees the whole colour budget
  • Strong first impression
  • Their cards are ~10% smaller
  • 3D transforms need a WebKit check
